**Answer: Yes, such a sequence exists.**

**Proof.**

Recall that the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ are countable and dense in $\mathbb{R}$. Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, there exists an enumeration of all rationals, i.e., a sequence $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that every rational number appears as some term $a_n$.

We claim this sequence has the desired property: for every real number $L$, there exists a subsequence $(a_{k_n})$ with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{k_n} = L$.

Let $L \in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary. We construct a subsequence converging to $L$ as follows.

For each $n \geq 1$, consider the open interval
$$I_n = \left(L - \tfrac{1}{n},\; L + \tfrac{1}{n}\right).$$

Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, each $I_n$ contains at least one rational number, hence at least one term of the sequence $(a_n)$.

We now pick indices $k_n$ inductively. Set $k_0 = 0$. Having chosen $k_0 < k_1 < \cdots < k_{n-1}$, since $I_n$ contains infinitely many rationals (in fact $I_n \cap \mathbb{Q}$ is infinite), but only finitely many of them appear among the terms $a_1, \dots, a_{k_{n-1}}$, there must exist some index $k_n > k_{n-1}$ with $a_{k_n} \in I_n$.

This produces a strictly increasing sequence of indices $(k_n)$ with
$$|a_{k_n} - L| < \frac{1}{n} \quad \text{for all } n \geq 1.$$

By the squeeze theorem, $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{k_n} = L$.

Since $L \in \mathbb{R}$ was arbitrary, the sequence $(a_n)$ — an enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}$ — satisfies the requirement that every real number is the limit of some subsequence. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
